text: People mostly think it's a safety measure for the moons, but forward contamination is the actual danger. Cassini spent 13 years in the Saturn system, picking up space dust and potential Earth microbes. If they parked it in a stable orbit, micrometeorites would eventually chip off pieces of the probe. Those chunks could land on Titan or Enceladus, introducing terrestrial bacteria to an ocean of liquid water. Crashing into Saturn's atmosphere burns the probe up and kills any surviving microbes. It's a deliberate burn-up. Much safer than letting it drift and take an unlucky hit from space junk.

A lot of this is just how skateboarding works mechanically. Every time you push, the leg that stays on the deck is doing most of the stabilizing work. It has to hold your weight, take the impact when the board settles down, and counterbalance while the other leg is in the air. Do that hundreds of times a session and that "stationary" leg gets hammered.

And here's the thing people rarely realize: most of us are right-footed or left-footed, so we keep pushing with the same leg. Over time the stabilizing side gets stronger than the pushing side, and then small imbalances build up in the hip, knee and even the ankles. You can't see it on a single practice session, but it accumulates. So if one leg hurts more than the other, that's not some mysterious injury, that's just the asymmetry from years of pushing with the dominant leg.

The pain is often in the hip flexors or the quads because those are the first to complain when you land repeatedly. The landing impact travels through the knee and into the hip. If it's more of a deep ache than a sharp twinge, it's probably muscular fatigue or mild strain, not a ligament issue. If it's sharp and localized, stop and give it a day or two.

The fix is stupidly simple. Alternate the pushing leg every few pushes, and deliberately practice pushing with your weaker side. For someone who's used to one side, this feels awful at first, but your stabilizing leg will stop getting all of the repetitive loading. Add in a bit of strengthening for the hip and knee stabilizers too. A couple of minutes of side leg raises and glute bridges will help your stationary leg handle the landing loads better.

Mostly it's a matter of breaking your one-sided habit before your hip or knee starts sending warning signs.

It's a descent label, not a residence one. That's what trips people up. For most Black Americans the connection is ancestry, usually through the transatlantic slave trade, which moved millions from West and Central Africa to North America starting in the 1600s. So 'Afro-American' points to that historical root, not where anyone currently lives. I find it kind of odd that the question treats 'African' as if it has to mean born there. In American usage it doesn't. The term also gets tangled because African American and Afro-American are used a bit differently. The older, historically rooted African American is the standard form, while Afro-American is a variant some use loosely. Black American is broader and includes newer immigrants and their children. Hence the premise feels off, because you can be Black in the US without ever having lived in Africa. The label is about inherited origin, and that's not the same as a current passport. People of African descent in the US is what the shorthand actually refers to.

In Syria, most weapons don't arrive by one grand channel. They leak out of army depots, are captured from opponents, smuggled across borders, and sometimes made locally. People still get them because the state is weak enough that guns feel necessary, not optional. After years of fighting, having a weapon is less about ideology and more about keeping your door locked and your family off the front lines. The supply chain is not mysterious, which is kind of wild. Local traders and black-market brokers have built a small but efficient supply web. No central army can claim full control.

Let’s get one thing straight first: not all drugs are "bad" in the same sense. The idea that a drug can give you intense euphoria with literally zero adverse effects is a fantasy, but that doesn't mean every dose of coke or heroin is a mistake. It depends on what "adverse" means to you, and for how long you use it. 

Why does the body insist on taking a cut from the pleasure? Because the reward system is a balancing machine. Your brain has baseline dopamine and endorphin levels that keep you going. When you inject or smoke a substance, you’re forcing that system into overdrive. The brain doesn't like being hijacked. It has to compensate. That’s why you feel so high in the moment, but you pay for it afterward with withdrawal, or a crash. You can’t just plug in pure happiness without the body reacting. It’s a homeostatic response.

So can there be a drug with 0 adverse effects? If by adverse you mean "no side effects, no crash, no dependence," then no, that drug doesn't really exist. To get the intense euphoria of heroin or cocaine, you need to hit the receptors hard and fast. But hitting receptors hard and fast means the brain will downregulate them. You’re basically training your brain to rely on the external chemical for the reward it’s supposed to produce on its own. That’s the core of addiction. The brain’s adaptation is the adverse effect you can’t avoid with anything that hits that hard.

Where people get tripped up is mixing up "bad" with "harmful." Some drugs (like alcohol or caffeine) are mild, and many people manage them well. Heroin and coke are intense, and that intensity is exactly what makes them risky. You can use them without becoming an addict, but the risk of the brain’s self-correction is always in the background. People still argue about whether a single line of coke is "bad." It depends on what you count as a downside, and whether you count the time, money, and the subtle shifts in your baseline mood.

And yeah, the "0 adverse effects" idea assumes you can just take the good part and leave the bad part behind. That’s not how neurochemistry works. You can’t have a drug that floods your reward system without the system recalibrating itself. So the pleasure is real, but it comes with a price. The trick isn't finding a magic pill, it's understanding how the system self-corrects. If you chase the high, the brain fights back, and that’s the adverse effect you can't skip.

Hi,
It’s real, and you’re not making it up. This sounds like sensory overload mixed with physical strain. A long shopping day means crowds, bright lights, constant decisions, standing for hours, and carrying bags. That combination can leave you feeling physically sore and completely off. Some people get this from the sensory environment alone, even if they barely move. Running low on food or water, or standing with bad posture, only makes it worse. If it keeps happening, get it checked. Try eating early, drinking water, and taking short breaks before the pain spikes, and if it gets severe, don’t tough it out.
— Sam

Hey,

I’d bet your brain grabbed milk because it’s the thing people most associate with cows. The question isn’t asking what cows give; it’s asking what they drink, and water is the plain fact. Still, if you were thinking about the silk part or feeling distracted, the milk word can leak in easily. That earlier bit, saying and spelling silk, sounds like he’s checking whether you can follow simple commands, not like a full diagnostic. If you answered milk just once and then corrected it, I wouldn’t overthink it. If it was a prank, he’s testing whether you’ll catch on. If it wasn’t, the milk answer is the part to pay attention to. If mixing things up continued or you noticed it more often, I’d tell a doctor about it and what happened.

Sam

Hey Sam,

I've been through this enough to know which questions actually save money later. First, get your finances in order before you start hunting. That means checking your credit report, knowing your debt-to-income ratio, and getting pre-approval rather than just a quote. Lenders approve based on your full picture, not just your income.

Second, walk the house at different times. A sunny morning shows nothing. Go at night and after rain, and you'll see damp spots, noisy neighbours, and whether the roof leaks. Those little details cost a lot to fix.

Also, don't let your lender's valuation be your ceiling. Ask about the mortgage rate, how long the fixer-upper project takes, and whether the bank will actually lend. A cheap house that fails appraisal is still expensive.

And insurance is the part that surprises people. Some insurers exclude houses in flood zones. Ask before you fall in love with a fixer-upper. Write down any cracks or stains, and ask the seller for maintenance records.

I'd start by picking out two or three houses with a mortgage broker, then go see them all in one day. That gives you a fair comparison. Send the actual questions and I can be more specific.

Best,
Alex

Hi,

It’s really just a lot of chemistry, not magic. The main difference is that a 3-in-1 bodywash/shampoo/conditioner has to work on both your skin and your hair, so the formula uses a high load of gentle surfactants. These create the thick foam you see. A regular shampoo just washes hair, and a regular body wash just cleans skin. The 3-in-1 is a compromise. It’s designed to not strip your skin’s natural oils, which is why it’s gentler than a standard shampoo.

A 2-in-1 shampoo/conditioner is a completely different animal. It combines cleansing and conditioning in one step, using a different balance of surfactants. It’s basically shampoo with conditioners added so you don’t need a separate bottle. People get confused by the numbers, but the 3-in-1 is an all-body product, while the 2-in-1 is strictly for hair.

You can read the ingredient list on the bottle to see the exact differences. The order of ingredients goes from most to least, so the first one is always water, followed by the main cleaning agent.

Best,
David

Hi,
Plate speed is measured mostly with GPS stations fixed to bedrock. The coordinates change by a few centimetres a year. You don't see that from day to day. You have to subtract the drift over months or years. That gives you a velocity. The raw fix is too noisy to use by itself. So they run a network of permanent stations, plus other geodetic methods, and combine them with plate models from earthquake data. You also have satellite laser ranging and VLBI, which check the GPS numbers against a global frame.
That's basically how they know, for example, that Africa moves about 2.5 cm per year relative to the rest of the world. The numbers are small, but consistent across the continent. You can't tell from one measurement. The point is to get a lot of them, and then do the maths on them. The result isn't just for one country. It's a network effect. So the speed comes out in centimetres a year, not metres. A single station, observed over months, contributes a small part of the picture.
It's not like watching a continent slide. It's a long record of positions. The speed isn't read off a single GPS fix.
Best,
Alex

Close relatives share ancestors, so when they have children, the offspring has a higher chance of inheriting the same variant from both sides. Most harmful genetic changes are recessive and sit quietly in carriers. Related parents are more likely to pass on the same rare bad allele from a common ancestor, making it homozygous. Once two copies are present, a deleterious effect can be expressed. A child from distant relatives may show a smaller effect; close cousins have a measurable one.

This matters for IQ because many of those variants affect brain development, synaptic function, or gene regulation. More homozygosity means a larger load of hidden harmful alleles is revealed at once. It is not a single IQ gene, and not every affected child is below average, but across many offspring the average tends to fall. The effect comes from unmasking recessive damage, not from mixing blood in the folklore sense.

Pain from an arm injury is often lower because the upper arm doesn't carry the same nerve density as the face, hands, or feet. Fingertips have so many sensory endings that a cut feels sharp; the upper arm is comparatively dull. Muscle and fat in the arm also spread out the force of a hit or the channel of a blade, so the injury is buffered rather than hitting bone or a dense nerve directly. What actually drives pain is how much tissue is disturbed, how close the wound is to a major nerve, and how the brain interprets the signal. A shallow graze on the biceps can feel mild, even if the same depth on the palm would be far worse. A deeper cut that hits the radial or ulnar nerve can hurt far more than the cliché suggests. The brain matters, too. Adrenaline during a shot or stab can blunt the signal, so a new colleague should treat "arms hurt less" as a tendency, with exceptions.

Carbon monoxide is so poisonous while carbon dioxide is just a normal byproduct because of how they treat your hemoglobin. Which is kind of wild given both contain carbon. CO2 is the exhaust from your body's metabolism, and your lungs vent it out without much effort. CO, on the other hand, binds to hemoglobin roughly 200 to 250 times more tightly than oxygen. It essentially steals the oxygen binding sites, forming a complex called carboxyhemoglobin. So your blood carries the toxin around while your organs starve for oxygen.

Why doesn't CO2 just stay stuck to the same sites? The two oxygen atoms in CO2 let it react with water and an enzyme called carbonic anhydrase, turning it into bicarbonate. That means it stays dissolved in the blood plasma and gets cleared in the lungs. 
Most of us take CO2 for granted because it is the chemical byproduct of cellular respiration. Your body produces it constantly, and a healthy pulmonary system exchanges it with the atmosphere efficiently. CO, however, is mostly from incomplete combustion. It doesn't get metabolized quickly. It has to be breathed out slowly, so exposure keeps building. In a confined space with poor ventilation, the concentration spikes. 

The bigger trap with CO is that it doesn't set off the body's natural breathing alarms. Your brainstem relies on high CO2 levels to tell you to take deeper breaths. CO is colorless and odorless. You can sit in a room with lethal CO levels for hours without realizing it, because the air feels fine. 
I always assumed CO was just a bad version of CO2, but it's not. CO2 is a useful chemical signal; CO is a physical blocker of your oxygen transport. People still argue about whether breathing a lot of CO2 is good for athletes' endurance, but that's a separate discussion from CO's immediate danger. 

If you work near combustion equipment or garages, install a CO alarm. The gas sneaks up to 35 percent of the hemoglobin binding sites before symptoms like headaches and dizziness start, and by the time you feel terrible, oxygen delivery is already significantly impaired. It causes silent oxygen starvation, earning its "silent killer" reputation.

In an airplane, the brace position is a small, awkward crouch that can save your life. When a plane hits rough air or the ground, your body keeps moving forward even after the aircraft stops suddenly. The brace asks you to fold forward, lower the head, keep the feet flat, and hold your knees or the seat in front of you. That shape does two useful things. It reduces the stress on the spine and neck, because the impact force is spread into bent legs and the seat rather than through a straight back. It also keeps the head away from hard surfaces and helps hold the chest and abdomen together, so internal organs are less likely to shift or tear.

It is like tucking your knees into a car crash, but adapted to airplane seats. The position is not glamorous and it feels unsafe, but it is one of the few things a passenger can actually control during an emergency. In practice, flight crews will call it over the intercom, and you simply crouch, grip what is nearest, and wait for the plane to come to rest. If you forget, you will remember it for a long time.

There are plenty of them. Companies with centuries of history do exist; it is just harder to get them in the news in a way that reaches a newcomer. The best-known example is the oldest continuously operating company in the world: Sumitomo, founded in 1567 in Osaka, Japan. It started as a merchant house that survived through the Meiji Restoration and the modernization of the country, and today it operates across energy, finance and industry. So the premise of the question is only half right. People simply remember the big tech names, which is understandable in the era of startups.

I'd take the bank loan, and here's why I do. The rate on the window sticker is the least reliable number in dealership financing. I have signed loan papers where the dealer printed 4.9% and the payment still didn't match what the bank would charge. That gap has almost nothing to do with interest and everything to do with the fees stacked around the loan.

A documentation fee, an origination fee, a prep charge, a service contract sold as protection. Add a $400 document fee and a $900 extended warranty to a $30,000 loan and the lower dealer APR is no longer lower once you include what you'll actually pay over 60 months. The bank's rate may sit a point or two higher, but it usually comes with a clean bill. I've seen bank payments that beat the dealer's quoted payment after all add-ons.

People also assume the dealer is the lender. Usually it isn't. The dealer brokers the loan through a third-party finance company, then charges for the convenience. "Convenience" can be worth money, but not always. If the bank can get you the same car without the extra costs, the headline rate isn't the whole story. The trick is comparing total cost, not the percentage on the page.

I still get why the low dealer rate is so tempting. It's the number you see first and the number everyone points at. But the total cost of the loan is what I care about, because it's the money I pay month after month. A small savings in fees can outweigh a bigger interest rate. That's why a 7.5% bank loan can beat a 6% dealer loan if the dealer stacks a $1,000 service contract and $350 in fees.

The other thing I'd check is whether the bank is the actual lender or also a broker. Some banks send you to a partner lender and charge you for arranging it. That arrangement can be more expensive than getting a loan straight from the lender.

What I'd want before signing anything is one sheet from each side with interest total and fee total printed on it. Then the answer to "which is cheaper" is just arithmetic.

I think states should keep deciding their own marijuana rules, and I’m mostly happy with the result. The country is a patchwork, with some states treating adult-use cannabis as legal, others allowing only medical access, and several still sitting in the middle. I also like that states can test different rules and see what works. What bugs me is federal law calling marijuana illegal. A dispensary in a legal state can still be charged under federal law, which is kind of wild. I can understand why states like California and Colorado moved first, with state politics and tax revenue pulling them forward. I don’t want Washington D.C. setting one rule for everyone. What I want is a simple federal rule that lets state laws operate without interference. Until then, people with state permits and cannabis businesses plan around that risk.

I find it kind of wild that the whole electrical story is just ions sliding around, not magic lightning. In your nerves, a resting neuron holds a voltage difference because potassium stays mostly inside while sodium stays mostly outside. When it fires, sodium channels open and charge floods in; that's the spark that lets a signal zip down the axon. Your heart does something related: a pacemaker area automatically generates rhythmic electrical waves. The details are boring, the result isn't.

I'm not a fan of songs whose whole point is a chopped-up 80s hook dropped on a new beat. Give me a producer who takes a line of melody, buries it under fresh instrumentation, and makes you work to find where it came from.

The interesting part of sampling is the context shift. When Daft Punk made "Harder, Better, Faster, Stronger," they used the opening riff from Van Halen's "Temptation," and that riff sounds completely different stripped of its original rock setting. A few years later Kanye West built "Stronger" directly off that Daft Punk track, so now you've got a chain: Van Halen, Daft Punk, then Kanye. Each step changes what the sample means. The same fragment is no longer the same thing once it's moved somewhere its original writers never intended.

That's the craft. You have to choose a piece that still works as a fragment, not a whole song. A whole-song sample is basically the song again. What makes it interesting is a two-second slice of guitar, a half-second vocal chop, a bass line you can't identify. I keep meaning to keep a list of the samples I spot first time and the ones I miss. The ones I miss are usually better hidden, and that's the point of a good producer.

People get annoyed at sampling because the new track sounds like the old one in disguise. I get the grumbling, but a great sample lives in the disguise. It should be recognizable only if you already know the source, and that's a fair trade. If the sample is blindingly obvious in the first three seconds, you've not earned my attention.

I'm also skeptical of the "sample flip" trend, where the new song is built from the old song's hook almost intact and the production is thin. There's nothing wrong with that if the beat and arrangement are actually strong, but a lot of it is just lazy recycling. I can tell in about ten seconds whether a producer added something or just copied.

What I'm looking for is the moment the old song's context breaks. A line of melody from a 1970s disco record played as a dark electronic pulse becomes something new, and the listener is left wondering where that tune came from. That wondering is the value. The sample isn't a theft, it's a conversation across decades, and the producer is the one keeping it honest.

My head hurts when I get a headache because the brain itself doesn't feel pain. It has literally zero pain receptors. So when I get those throbbing, one-sided aches on my temple, it's not the brain throwing a tantrum. It's the packaging. The meninges (the membranes covering the brain), the blood vessels in the scalp, or the tight muscles in my neck get irritated, inflamed, or spasm.

I always assumed a headache meant my brain was literally breaking. But it's just the scaffolding. Dehydration, skipping a night's sleep, or a sudden drop in blood pressure can make those outer tissues swell and spasm.

Those tension headaches from staring at a screen for eight hours are just my neck and scalp muscles locking up. The migraines are a whole different beast. I think the blood vessels around my head start pulsing in time with my heartbeat, and the pain throbs aggressively. The skull feels like it's being squeezed from the inside. The brain is just along for the ride, completely unaware that its own packaging is in agony.

I still don't know if the food is good. We never got to eat. We showed up at 7:20 p.m. on Sunday, picking this place because of our 10:00 p.m. show at the same hotel, and assumed the evening would be simple. They had us put our names on their completely useless digital waitlist. At 8:23 p.m. they told us to come back for payment. We went and stood there until 8:40 p.m., when staff mentioned we probably wouldn't be seated until 9:15 p.m. Just two of us, and they offered zero fixes. If a wait stretches that far beyond paying, why not say it upfront so the night isn't entirely blown? Absolute disaster. Would be zero stars if I could rate it that low.

I went to this buffet on a Friday around 4:30 p.m., and, surprisingly, there was no line at all. For two people, it came out to about $130, which felt pretty steep. Before going, I figured the price would be comparable to a steakhouse. Afterward, I learned the buffet actually cost a little more than what I'd have expected to pay at one.

I was disappointed that there wasn't any steak. At that price, I'd assumed there would be some kind of steak option. The meat choices were lamb, prime rib and chicken, but that's the kind of thing you can find at other Las Vegas buffets for a lot less money.

The seafood station had Alaskan crab legs and rock crab claws. Alaskan legs are at a lot of Vegas buffets, but I hadn't run into rock crab claws anywhere else, so those were interesting. The problem was there were no crab-claw crackers. Staff said wooden mallets were available, but our table was so close to the next one that I didn't want to start smashing shells and send pieces flying at the people next to us. So I just ate the crab legs.

The Asian station wasn't especially distinctive. It reminded me quite a bit of the buffet at Rampart Casino. Dessert had gelato and pastries, but nothing really stood out. Fresh juices were offered, although I didn't try any.

Taking it all in, I'd call the place acceptable, but overpriced for what it offers. If you're curious, it's worth trying once, especially if there's no wait. But if the line is long, I'd probably reconsider it.

Four stars, and I'm keeping it.
The space bar rattles like a loose pen cap in a drawer when I hit it with my thumb. The E key also repeats now and then, so "example" becomes "eexample" and I have to backspace. It happens maybe once an afternoon, always when I'm typing fast and not looking.

I paid $38 and kept it anyway, because of the switches. I asked the seller what they were, and the answer took a week. By then I had already pulled off a keycap and found out that they were brown tactile switches, with a small bump under the finger and a soft landing at the bottom. My old membrane board felt like pressing wet cardboard by comparison.

My job is mostly email, often two or three hours in a row, and my wrists don't ache by the end anymore. That mattered more than the rattle.

Sending it back would have meant paying for postage and boxing it up, and I'd have been without a keyboard while I waited. So it stays on the desk, and I tap the space bar a little closer to the middle now.

I’ve been to Vegas almost my whole life, well, the under-21 parts, so I’ve watched plenty of shows before I could bet. Le Rêve at the Wynn is one I finally caught, and it was mixed, maybe a little worse than mixed. The circular stage was the part that worked for me. You are essentially looking down into it, so nearly every seat gives you a decent view, which is uncommon in Vegas. Some individual acts are good, especially the strength pieces, the aerialists, and the divers. Those people are genuinely athletes. But much of it felt familiar because I thought of Cirque du Soleil. Not exactly a copy, just that if you have seen Cirque, you have seen similar feats, sometimes with more clarity. Clarity is where this show fell short for me. What is the story? There is a dream, maybe? A man? Water? It felt like a string of pretty images, and the show never told me what it wanted to say. There was also too much happening at once. Too many people and elements, and too many wow moments stacked one after another. A smaller, more restrained version would have landed harder. This had the familiar Vegas impulse to make more better, so they packed in everything. One practical note. If you are staying at Wynn or Encore, they offer a deal, $99 instead of the usual $125, which helps. Would I see it again? Probably not, and I wouldn’t pay a second time. Aside from a few stunts, it was average. I wasn’t blown away, and I didn’t think the audience was either. Still, a few friends liked it, and if you have never seen it, try it once, just do not expect to be overwhelmed.

About two years ago, we ordered two shirts for my father from Rockmount Ranch Wear by phone. The sales rep got the address wrong: her handwritten 7 read as a 1, so what should have been 5407 went to 5401. The people at 5401 took the package to the local UPS store to send it back. It just vanished; we never saw or heard about it again. It took us several weeks to notice. During the dispute, we ordered two more shirts. Rockmount refused to refund the original two; at that stage the owner handled it. He admitted the shipment went to the wrong address but said no refund until the shirts came back. He even claimed we were partly to blame because we hadn't been friendly enough to the people at 5401, four doors away. We disputed the original charge with our credit card company and eventually got a credit.
